t.1.217.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those two tigers among men, stationed on their two chariots on both sides of the forest fire, wrought a great slaughter of creatures in all directions.
t.1.217.2: For wherever the creatures dwelling in Khāṇḍava were seen fleeing, there the two heroes rushed about after them.
t.1.217.4: But as the Khāṇḍava was burning, creatures in their thousands then flew up, uttering terrible cries in all ten directions.
t.1.217.3: For because of the swift motion of the chariots they could see no gap between them; those two chariot-warriors, the best of car-fighters, appeared as though whirled about in a circle.
t.1.217.6: Some, embracing their sons, and others their fathers and mothers, could not abandon them out of love, and so met their death just as they were.
t.1.217.5: Many were burnt in part of their bodies, and others were thoroughly scorched; with their eyes burst open, broken apart, scattering in flight, they were bereft of their senses.
t.1.217.7: Others, with distorted appearances, flew up by the thousands; reeling here and there, they fell back into the fire.
t.1.217.8: Here and there living creatures could be seen perishing, their wings, eyes and feet burnt, writhing upon the surface of the earth.
t.1.217.9: As all the waters in their places were being brought to the boil, O Bhārata, turtles and fish were seen by the thousands, bereft of life.
t.1.217.10: With their bodies blazing, the living creatures in that forest, at the moment their lives were ending, were seen like fires that had taken bodily form.
t.1.217.11: As they flew up in this way, Pārtha cut them to pieces with his arrows and then, laughing, hurled them into the blazing fire whose path is black.
t.1.217.12: Their whole bodies studded with arrows, they let out great cries, flew swiftly upward, and fell back into the fire.
t.1.217.13: The cry of the forest-dwellers, struck by arrows and being burned, was heard like the roar of the ocean as it is being churned.
t.1.217.15: Then all the great-souled dwellers of heaven went for refuge to the king of the gods, the thousand-eyed Puraṃdara.
t.1.217.14: And from the delighted, great-flamed Fire, flames leapt up into the sky and caused very great alarm among the dwellers of heaven.
t.1.217.17: Having heard that from them, and having seen it for himself as well, the slayer of Vṛtra, whose steeds are bay horses, set out to deliver the Khāṇḍava forest.
t.1.217.16: Why are all these humans being burned by the black-trailed Fire? Surely the destruction of the worlds has not arrived, O lord of the immortals?
t.1.217.19: Then the thousand-eyed one, releasing streams as thick as axles by the hundreds of thousands, rained down upon the fire in the direction of Khāṇḍava.
t.1.217.20: But those torrents, never reaching it, were dried up in the very sky by the blazing energy of Jātavedas; not a single one of them reached Pāvaka.
t.1.217.22: Bound all about by streams of flame and filled with smoke and lightning, that forest became dreadful, resounding as with the roar of thunder.
t.1.217.21: Then the slayer of Namuci, greatly enraged at the blazing one, once again rained down upon him, pouring forth abundant water.
t.1.217.18: Covering the sky with a vast net of clouds of many forms, the wielder of the thunderbolt, lord of the gods, poured down rain.
